sections.b: Psalm 151 tells, in David's voice, how the small, youngest son who kept his father's sheep and made his own instruments was chosen over his tall brothers, anointed, and given victory over the Philistine, whose own sword cut off his head (Psalm 151:1–7). Its heading calls it David's "in his own hand" and "outside the count."

Psalm 151, printed after Psalm 150 in the Greek Psalter, puts David's choosing in his own mouth: "Among my brothers I was small, the youngest of my father's household" (Psalm 151:1; compare 1 Samuel 16:11), "My brothers were good-looking and big, but the Lord took no delight in them" (Psalm 151:5; compare 1 Samuel 16:6–10). The Hebrew form in the Qumran Psalms Scroll (11Q5) adds that God "made me leader of his people and ruler over the children of his covenant."

Psalm 151's heading sets it "when he fought Goliath man to man." It tells the duel in two lines: the Philistine "called down curses on me by his idols" (Psalm 151:6; 1 Samuel 17:43), and "I drew his own sword and cut off his head, and I lifted shame off the Israelites" (Psalm 151:7; 1 Samuel 17:26, 51). It leaves out the sling and the stone. The second Hebrew poem in 11Q5, "the beginning of David's mighty deeds," breaks off as David sees "a Philistine taunting from the ranks of the Philistines."

The Greek Psalter ends with a psalm "outside the number" (Psalm 151:0), and a Hebrew form of it stands near the end of the Psalms Scroll from Qumran (11Q5), with a prose note that David wrote 4,050 psalms and songs. Orthodox and Coptic Psalters keep it; Catholic and Protestant Bibles count 150 psalms (Council of Trent, "a hundred and fifty psalms").

sections.h: "In his own hand, outside the number"
sections.b: Psalm 151's Greek heading is unlike any other title: "written in David's own hand" (idiographos), "outside the count," "when he fought Goliath man to man" (Psalm 151:0). The Hebrew form in 11Q5 has a plain title, "Hallelujah. Of David son of Jesse," and gives its second poem its own heading, "The beginning of David's mighty deeds."

Psalm 151 begins with David the shepherd (Psalm 151:1) and has God take him "from my father's sheep" to anoint him (Psalm 151:4), as Psalm 78:70–71 and 2 Samuel 7:8 say. The Hebrew form in 11Q5 says "he made me shepherd of his flock and ruler over his young goats," without naming who.

"My hands made an instrument; my fingers tuned a harp" (Psalm 151:2). The Hebrew form in 11Q5 names a pipe (ʿugav) and a lyre (kinnor), the same pair as Jubal's in Genesis 4:21, and adds, "and I gave glory to the LORD." Compare Amos 6:5, "like David they design musical instruments of their own."

Psalm 151:4 says God "anointed me with the oil of his anointing"; some Greek manuscripts slip into "the mercy of his anointing." The Hebrew form in 11Q5 has "holy oil," the words of Psalm 89:20, and has Samuel the prophet do the anointing, as 1 Samuel 16:13 does.

The Greek Psalm 151 says God "sent out his angel" to anoint David (Psalm 151:4); the Hebrew form in 11Q5 says "he sent his prophet to anoint me, Samuel," and its second poem speaks of the time "after the prophet of God had anointed him."
Psalm 151:6 calls Goliath ho allophylos, "the foreigner," the Greek Bible's usual word for a Philistine; the Hebrew form in 11Q5 says "a Philistine ... from the ranks of the Philistines."

Psalm 151 sets the tall brothers whom God passed over (Psalm 151:5) beside the Philistine champion whom the small shepherd beheaded with his own sword (Psalm 151:6–7). It never mentions Goliath's height, which 1 Samuel 17:4 gives; the contrast is between big and small, not a measurement.
Where 1 Samuel 17:43 says Goliath "called down curses on David by his gods," Psalm 151:6 says "by his idols" (eidōla), the Greek Bible's scornful word for false gods.

sections.h: Psalm 151: in the Psalter, outside the number
sections.b: Psalm 151 calls itself "outside the count" (Psalm 151:0). Orthodox Psalters print it after Psalm 150 with that label, and the Coptic Orthodox Church reads it on Bright Saturday (the day before the Resurrection feast); the Council of Trent defined a Psalter "consisting of a hundred and fifty psalms"; the KJV Apocrypha does not include it. Before the Psalms Scroll from Qumran (11Q5) was found in 1956, no Hebrew text of it was known.
